analysis.one_liner: Bans U.S. gasoline exports whenever domestic pump prices stay above a set threshold.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first referral in committee, with no cosponsors and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the President to block exports of American-made gasoline whenever the national average price stayed at or above $3.12 a gallon for a week straight, keeping that fuel in the domestic market during price spikes. The President could exempt exports deemed in the national interest. The idea was to hold more supply at home so that gasoline prices at the pump would not climb as high when prices spike.
analysis.who_benefits: American drivers and businesses that buy gasoline, who would see a larger share of domestically refined fuel kept in the U.S. market during periods when prices exceed the trigger, which could put downward pressure on pump prices during spikes.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President to prohibit exporting gasoline produced in the United States during any period when the national average price has been $3.12 or higher per gallon for seven straight days, ending when it stays below that level for seven days.
Keeps fuel refined in the U.S. available to American buyers during price spikes rather than allowing it to be sold to overseas buyers.
Gives the President authority to exempt exports consistent with the national interest, allowing flexibility if a ban would cause other problems.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. oil refiners and gasoline exporters, who would lose the ability to sell domestically produced gasoline to foreign buyers during high-price periods, cutting into export revenue. Consumers could also face unintended consequences if reduced export revenue over time discourages domestic refining investment.

drawbacks.text: Gasoline prices are set in a global market, so holding exports back does not guarantee lower pump prices, and the ban could reduce refiners' profit margins enough to discourage investment in domestic refining capacity, potentially tightening supply later.

The $3.12 trigger is a fixed number that national average prices were frequently above in recent years, so the ban could have been in effect for long stretches rather than only during emergencies, making it function more like a near-permanent export restriction than a price-spike safety valve.
The President's broad exemption authority means enforcement would depend heavily on each administration's judgment of what is in the national interest, making the guarantee to consumers uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it worked as intended, drivers would get relief at the pump during price spikes, at the cost of export profits for refiners. But the design carries real risks: a fixed low trigger could keep the ban in force almost continuously, and cutting refiners' export access could shrink domestic refining capacity over time, working against the goal of cheaper gasoline. The bill never got enough support to test these tradeoffs in a debate or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Gasoline Export Ban Act of 2022 in the House on November 7, 2022.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs the same day.
No cosponsors signed on, and no further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. refiners and gasoline exporters, who kept unrestricted access to foreign markets, and no consumer relief at the pump was enacted. The outcome leaves pump prices during spikes to be set without an export restriction in place.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House and referred it to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

against.name: House Foreign Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote during the remaining session.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so there is no roll-call record to show how support or opposition split by party; the single sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.note: During high-price periods the bill would cut off their ability to sell U.S.-refined gasoline abroad, reducing export revenue. Their interest in continuing unrestricted exports ran against cheaper domestic pump prices. They faced no loss, since the bill never became law.
Keeping export-eligible gasoline in the domestic market during price spikes could put downward pressure on pump prices. They gained nothing because the bill died.
